newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Eight novels shortlisted for Dublin literary award.
newsitem.headline: Eight novels shortlisted for Dublin literary award.

text.p: The International IMPAC Dublin Literary Award said on Tuesday that eight novels had been shortlisted for this year's award, the world's largest prize for a single work of fiction.

The contenders for the 100,000 punt ($154,000) award include two U.S. novels, "Reservation Blues" by Sherman Alexie and A.J. Verdelle's "The Good Negress", a tale of a young black girl in a poor family in rural Virginia in the 1960s.
Representing Europe are Scotland's Alan Warner with his novel "Morvern Callar" and "A Heart So White" by Javier Marias from Spain.
Also on the shortlist are Italy's Antonio Tabucchi with "Declares Pereira" and Sweden's Lars Gustafsson with "A Tilers' Afternoon".

Duong Thu Huong's novel about the Vietnam War, "Novel Without a Name", and Rohinton Mistry's "A Fine Balance," set in India in the 1970s and shortlisted for the 1996 Booker prize are the Asian contenders for the prize.
The 1997 shortlist was selected by an international panel of judges from 113 novels nominated by 104 libraries in 49 countries around the world.

The winner will be chosen by a panel chaired by U.S. historian Allen Weinstein and made up of British writer Margaret Drabble, Irish poet Nuala Ni Dhomhnaill, Czech novelist Josef Skvorecky, Canadian novelist Jane Urquhart and U.S. writer Shawn Wong and will be announced on May 14.
Australian novelist David Malouf was the first winner of prize last year for his novel "Remembering Babylon".
The award is sponsored by the productivity improvement company IMPAC and administered by Dublin City Library and aims to capitalise on Dublin's literary reputation.

The city boasts three Nobel literature prize winners this century - William Butler Yeats, George Bernard Shaw and Samuel Beckett - while 1995 winner Seamus Heaney, originally from Northern Ireland, lives in the Irish capital.

The nominations are made by libraries around the world in a bid to keep the award free of influence from publishers, book-sellers, critics and other commercial interests, the organisers say. ($ = 0.648 Irish Pounds)
